## Two layers in every note you'll ever play

A first program should do more than prove the speakers work. This one also
introduces the split that the whole book rests on: the notes and timings
describe a phrase, and the synth gives that phrase a body. Change either one
without touching the other.

The six-note phrase below rises from E, turns at B, and comes home. Pitches live
in one array, durations in another, and `play_phrase` zips them together and
hands each pair to the synth. Start with `:pluck`, because its fast attack makes
every onset easy to locate. You'll hear exactly where the notes begin before
you've decided anything about their colour.

Listen for two things separately. First follow the shape of the phrase. Then
listen to the edge and the tail of each note. Shape belongs to the score. Edge
and tail belong mostly to the synth.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

notes = [:e3, :g3, :a3, :b3, :a3, :e3]
durations = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |pitches, lengths|
  pitches.zip(lengths).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

play_phrase notes, durations
```

Six evenly spaced attacks. The first four climb, the fifth turns back down, and
the last E lasts twice as long as anything before it. That extra beat is what
makes the ending sound like an ending, and `:pluck` leaves clean gaps between
the attacks so you can count them.

## Change the instrument, not the notes

1. Swap `:pluck` for `:prophet` and run it again. Not one note or sleep has
   changed, so anything different you hear belongs to the instrument. You lose
   the click of each onset; you gain a tail long enough to fill the gap before
   the next note. Same phrase, different body.

2. Put `:pluck` back, then try `:blade` and `:fm`, one at a time. How precisely
   can you locate each onset in each one? Use words like *sharp*, *blurred*,
   *dry* or *lingering* only when they name something you actually heard.

3. Back to the original synth, and change the final duration from `1` to `0.5`.
   The line still reaches the same E, but it no longer rests there. That's
   closure by pitch stripped of closure by time, and it's a much weaker ending.

## Where each job lives

The arrays are the score. One says which pitches happen, the other says how far
the musical clock moves after each one. `play_phrase` is the renderer, turning
those pairs into scheduled sound. And `use_synth` picks the generator. Because
each job has its own visible home, a one-word edit recolours the entire phrase
without touching its contour or its timing.

Three Sonic Pi calls do most of the work here. `play` starts a sound. `sleep`
advances this thread's musical clock before the next instruction runs.
`use_synth` sets the instrument for every later `play`. Here's the part that
catches programmers out: `play` doesn't wait for its note to finish. The waiting
is entirely `sleep`'s job, which means a note's audible tail and the distance to
the next onset are two different quantities that you control separately.

You can expose that gap without changing synths at all. Keep `:pluck` and change
`release` from `duration * 0.8` to `duration * 1.4`. The attacks still land on
the same half-beat grid, but every tail now runs past the next attack. The phrase
gets more connected because the renderer changed, not because the score did.

Keep the log pane in your loop. A misspelled synth name stops the program and
points at a line. A correctly spelled but unsuitable synth runs perfectly and
tells you nothing, because that's a judgement only your ears can make. Code
feedback confirms Sonic Pi understood you. It has no opinion about the music.

This boundary comes back constantly, because it keeps musical questions local.
Lesson 2 replaces the note names with integers and starts doing arithmetic on
them, and the playback loop won't need to change at all.

## Take it further

Write a second six-note phrase and pick four synths that show its contour in
four different ways. Keep exactly one `use_synth` line and one call to
`play_phrase`, so that changing a single symbol still swaps the instrument for
everything. If you can't do that, your score and your renderer have started to
leak into each other.

Then misspell a synth name on purpose and copy the log message down next to the
corrected line. Run all four valid synths in Sonic Pi 5, and for each one write a
concrete observation about attack or decay, plus whether the phrase's register
suits it. You'll finish with two reusable phrases, four synths you have opinions
about, and an error message you can now read at a glance.
